claim: At GC-PC synapses, sustained facilitation of synaptic transmission was observed up to the 25th-30th stimulus at frequencies above 50 Hz.
source: As already reported in rodent cerebellar slices (Kreitzer and Regehr, 2000), a sustained facilitation of synaptic transmission was observed up to the 25th-30th stimulus at frequencies above 50 Hz, indicating that the number of SVs released increased with stimulation frequency.
evidence: Experimental observation from slice recordings showing facilitation pattern during high-frequency stimulation

claim: The paired-pulse facilitation at the first interval increased with frequency at GC-PC synapses.
source: The paired-pulse facilitation at the first interval increased with frequency (paired-pulse facilitation EPSC2/EPSC1: 171.15% ± 10.03 at 50 Hz, n = 9, 215.96% ± 6.90 at 100 Hz, n = 27, Figure 1A).
evidence: Quantitative measurements from electrophysiological recordings showing frequency-dependent facilitation

claim: After 30 to 40 stimuli at high frequency, depression (EPSCn/EPSC1 < 1) was observed at GC-PC synapses.
source: After 30 to 40 stimuli, a depression (EPSCn/EPSC1 < 1) was observed.
evidence: Experimental observation from electrophysiological recordings

claim: The stimulation protocol did not evoke asynchronous release at GC-PC synapses.
source: The perfect superimposition of normalized charges and amplitudes at any stimulus number during 50 Hz and 2 Hz trains suggested that our stimulation protocol did not evoke asynchronous release (Figure 1A).
evidence: Analysis of charge/amplitude ratios showing no evidence of asynchronous release

claim: No difference was observed in the maximal recruitment of releasable SVs between 50 Hz and 100 Hz stimulation.
source: However, although initial facilitation during the first two or three pulses is higher at 10 ms than at 20 ms intervals (Valera et al., 2012) no difference was observed in the maximal recruitment of releasable SVs between 50 Hz and 100 Hz (number of quanta released per bouton at 50 Hz = 39.47 ± 2.75, n = 9 compared to 40.14 ± 7.50 at 100 Hz, n = 27, p=0.82, t-test, Figure 1B).
evidence: Statistical comparison of cumulative quantal release at different frequencies

claim: At 2 Hz stimulation, synaptic responses at GC-PC synapses did not facilitate during the first stimuli.
source: Conversely, at 2 Hz, the synaptic responses did not facilitate during the first stimuli (Figure 1A,C) and depressed rapidly after a mean delay of 7 stimuli ± 5 stimuli (n = 35) (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: Experimental observation from electrophysiological recordings at low frequency

claim: Low-frequency depression (LFD) at GC-PC synapses depressed rapidly after a mean delay of 7 stimuli ± 5 stimuli.
source: Conversely, at 2 Hz, the synaptic responses did not facilitate during the first stimuli (Figure 1A,C) and depressed rapidly after a mean delay of 7 stimuli ± 5 stimuli (n = 35) (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: Quantitative measurement of depression onset from experimental data

claim: EPSC amplitudes during low-frequency depression decreased mono-exponentially in the majority of cells recorded with a mean time constant of 15.9 s ± 1.2 s.
source: Strikingly, the EPSC amplitudes decreased mono-exponentially in the majority of cells recorded (n = 32) with a mean time constant of 15.9 s ± 1.2 s.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of depression kinetics from experimental recordings

claim: A lack of LFD was observed for approximately 12% of PCs recorded in the vermis.
source: A lack of LFD was observed for ~12% of PCs recorded in the vermis (5 cells out of 39 cells).
evidence: Statistical observation from experimental recordings

claim: APs are reliably initiated and transmitted along PFs at high frequencies and at physiologic temperature (35°C).
source: APs are reliably initiated and transmitted along PFs at high frequencies and at physiologic temperature (35°C) (Kreitzer and Regehr, 2000; Isope and Barbour, 2002; Baginskas et al., 2009).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple literature citations

claim: Impaired PF excitability did not cause LFD.
source: The lack of any significant change in the onset and the kinetics of depression after stimulating GC somata (Figure 1D,E) suggested that impaired PF excitability did not cause LFD.
evidence: Comparison of depression patterns between PF and GC soma stimulation

claim: The depression could be reliably induced in a given PC as long as the recording of EPSCs could be maintained.
source: While the onset and the plateau of LFD varied among PCs (Figure 1F), the depression could be reliably induced in a given PC as long as the recording of EPSCs could be maintained.
evidence: Observation from repeated experimental protocols

claim: EPSC amplitudes fully recovered after a resting period of 5 to 10 min following LFD.
source: EPSC amplitudes fully recovered after the resting period following the end of LFD#1 protocol and the time courses of EPSCs amplitude of LFD#1 LFD#2 were identical (Figure 1G,H).
evidence: Experimental observation from repeated LFD protocols with recovery periods

claim: A sustained stimulation at low frequency can almost completely silence the release apparatus of GC terminals.
source: Our findings reveal for a first time that a sustained stimulation at low frequency can almost completely silence the release apparatus of GC terminals.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental observations of LFD

claim: GCs fire spontaneously in a range of 0.4 to 10 Hz in vivo.
source: In vivo recordings have shown that GCs fire spontaneously in a range of 0.4 to 10 Hz (Chadderton et al., 2004; Jörntell and Ekerot, 2006).
evidence: Statement supported by in vivo recording studies from literature

claim: No change in the properties of LFD were observed after a shift in the firing frequency.
source: No change in the properties of LFD were observed after a shift in the firing frequency (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E) indicating that presynaptic terminals of GCs can filter a broad range of low-frequency activities of GCs.
evidence: Experimental observation from variable frequency stimulation protocols

claim: Presynaptic terminals of GCs can filter a broad range of low-frequency activities.
source: No change in the properties of LFD were observed after a shift in the firing frequency (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E) indicating that presynaptic terminals of GCs can filter a broad range of low-frequency activities of GCs.
evidence: Inference from experimental data showing consistent LFD across different low frequencies

claim: After a full blockage of synaptic transmission by LFD, glutamate release capacity recovered to 70.7 ± 7.6% within 10 ms during 100 Hz stimulation.
source: Strikingly, after a full blockage of synaptic transmission, the glutamate release capacity recovered to 70.7 ± 7.6% within 10 ms, reached a peak of amplitude after 5 to 8, and then declined progressively (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from recovery experiments

claim: A full recovery from LFD was achieved within 70 ms during 100 Hz stimulation.
source: After the 7th stimuli, EPSC amplitudes evoked by the 100 Hz recovery train reached values that were not significantly different from values observed at the same stimulus number in a control train elicited before LFD induction (Figure 2C,D). This suggests that a full recovery from LFD was achieved within 70 ms.
evidence: Statistical comparison of EPSC amplitudes between recovery and control conditions

claim: Mean amplitudes of EPSCs recorded during train at 50 Hz applied in control condition were not statistically different from those recorded after LFD induction within approximately 50 ms.
source: Mean amplitudes of EPSCs recorded during train at 50 Hz applied in control condition were not statistically different from those recorded after LFD induction (Figure 2E) within approximately 50 ms (5 stimuli).
evidence: Statistical comparison of EPSC amplitudes at 50 Hz

claim: With 20 Hz applied after LFD, the recovery was limited, and EPSC amplitudes were smaller than the ones recorded in control condition.
source: With 20 Hz applied after LFD, the recovery was limited, and EPSC amplitudes were smaller than the ones recorded in control condition (Figure 2F).
evidence: Experimental observation comparing recovery at 20 Hz to control

claim: The level of recovery after LFDtriplet was inversely proportional to the frequency of triplet stimulation.
source: Strikingly, the level of recovery after LFDtriplet was inversely proportional to the frequency of triplet stimulation (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: Experimental observation from LFDtriplet protocols at different frequencies

claim: When triplets frequency was set at 200 Hz during LFDtriplet, synaptic transmission hardly recovered (maximal recovery 38.9%±7.19 n = 6, compared to 196.7%±8.7, after LFD, n = 27).
source: For example, when triplets frequency was set at 200 Hz during LFDtriplet, synaptic transmission hardly recovered (maximal recovery 38.9%±7.19 n = 6, compared to 196.7%±8.7, after LFD, n = 27, Figure 3C).
evidence: Quantitative comparison of recovery between LFD and LFDtriplet protocols

claim: LFDtriplet stimulation depleted or disabled the population of SVs that support the recovery from LFD.
source: This finding suggested that LFDtriplet stimulation depleted or disabled the population of SVs that support the recovery from LFD.
evidence: Inference from experimental observation of reduced recovery after LFDtriplet

claim: The normalized cumulative EPSC amplitude was higher during LFDtriplet than during LFD (6440.9 ± 945% for LFD compared to 9353.5 ± 1199.9% for LFDtriplet, p<0.001, paired t test, n = 18).
source: The normalized cumulative EPSC amplitude was higher during LFDtriplet than during LFD (6440.9 ± 945% for LFD compared to 9353.5 ± 1199.9% for LFDtriplet, p<0.001, paired t test, n = 18, Figure 4C,D).
evidence: Statistical comparison of cumulative EPSC amplitudes between protocols

claim: When the cumulative EPSC amplitude measured during the recovery train was added, no significant differences were observed between LFD and LFDtriplet protocols.
source: When the cumulative EPSC amplitude measured during the recovery train was added, no significant differences were observed between the two protocols (11696.3 ± 1163.6% for LFD and recovery train compared to 11379.0 ± 1349.6% for LFDtriplet and recovery train, p=0.61, paired t test, n = 18, Figure 4C,D).
evidence: Statistical comparison of total cumulative release between protocols

claim: SVs recruited only during LFDtriplet or only during recovery train belong to the same reluctant pool.
source: This suggests that SVs recruited only during LFDtriplet or only during recovery train belong to the same reluctant pool.
evidence: Inference from cumulative release data showing equivalent total release

claim: The calculated number of quanta released during LFD was statistically lower than during LFDtriplet (42.7 ± 6.2 quanta for LFD compared to 60.8 ± 8.0 quanta for LFDtriplet, p<0.01, paired t-test, n = 18).
source: Accordingly, the calculated number of quanta released during LFD was statistically lower than during LFDtriplet (42.7 ± 6.2 quanta for LFD compared to 60.8 ± 8.0 quanta for LFDtriplet, p<0.01, paired t-test, n = 18, Figure 4E)
evidence: Statistical comparison of estimated quantal release

claim: The total number of quanta released during LFD and recovery train or LFDtriplet and recovery train were not significantly different (77.5 ± 7.7 quanta released for LFD and recovery train compared to 74.8 ± 8.9 quanta released for LFDtriplet and recovery, p=0.51, paired t-test, n = 18).
source: and the total number of quanta released during LFD and recovery train or LFDtriplet and recovery train were not significantly different (77.5 ± 7.7 quanta released for LFD and recovery train compared to 74.8 ± 8.9 quanta released for LFDtriplet and recovery, p=0.51, paired t-test, n = 18, Figure 4E).
evidence: Statistical comparison of total quantal release across protocols

claim: Releasable SVs in GC boutons segregate in two distinct pools: the fully-releasable pool that can be released by a single AP and a reluctant pool that can only be recruited during bursts of APs reaching frequencies ≥ 20 Hz.
source: These results suggest that releasable SVs in GC boutons segregate in two distinct pools: the fully-releasable pool that can be released by a single AP and a reluctant pool that can only be recruited during bursts of APs reaching frequencies ≥ 20 Hz.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations of frequency-dependent release

claim: Paired-pulse stimulation at high frequencies applied during LFD induced strikingly high PPR values.
source: Paired-pulse stimulation at high frequencies applied during LFD induced strikingly high PPR values (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,C).
evidence: Experimental observation from paired-pulse protocols during LFD

claim: Strikingly high PPR values were observed whatever was the percentage of inhibition and regardless of the timing of LFD.
source: These strikingly high PPR values were observed whatever was the percentage of inhibition and regardless of the timing of LFD (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Experimental observation from variable timing paired-pulse protocols

claim: The status of the fully-releasable pool does not influence the mobilization of the reluctant pool.
source: These findings strongly suggest that the status of the fully-releasable pool does not influence the mobilization of the reluctant pool.
evidence: Inference from PPR data showing consistent recruitment regardless of depression state

claim: SVs can be recruited from a reluctant pool into a fully-releasable pool on a millisecond timescale.
source: They further suggest that SVs can be recruited from a reluctant pool into a fully-releasable pool on a millisecond timescale.
evidence: Inference from experimental data showing rapid recovery kinetics

claim: During high-frequency stimulation (100 Hz), residual Ca2+ sums linearly during 50 stimuli, building up to a steady state amplitude of approximately 2 µM.
source: During high-frequency stimulation (100 Hz), this residual Ca2+ sums linearly during 50 stimuli (Brenowitz and Regehr, 2007), building up to a steady state amplitude of ~2 µM.
evidence: Modeling result based on literature values for Ca2+ dynamics

claim: During low-frequency stimulation (2 Hz), residual Ca2+ dropped back to its resting level between pulses and recruited SVs returned to the reluctant pool between stimuli.
source: On the other hand, during low-frequency stimulation (2 Hz), residual Ca2+ dropped back to its resting level between pulses and recruited SVs returned to the reluctant pool between stimuli.
evidence: Modeling result explaining low-frequency depression mechanism

claim: The sequential two-pool model with Ca2+-dependent recruitment reproduced rapid recovery from LFD followed by facilitation.
source: Renewed driving of the depressed model at high-frequency reproduced a rapid recovery from LFD and was followed by facilitation (Figure 6D compared with Figure 2), thus illustrating the recruitment of the reluctant pool.
evidence: Modeling results compared to experimental data

claim: The single pool model and parallel pool model predict a depression of release during high-frequency stimulation and a strong facilitation during sustained low-frequency stimulation.
source: In both models, the pools are replenished at a fixed rate independent of Ca2+. Both models predict a depression of release during high-frequency stimulation and a strong facilitation during sustained low-frequency stimulation (Figure 6F,G).
evidence: Modeling results from alternative models

claim: The single pool and parallel pool models cannot explain the release mechanisms at GC-PC synapses.
source: The latter two models successfully described several aspects of release at the depressing calyx of Held synapse that operates with a very large RRP (Sätzler et al., 2002) but cannot explain the release mechanisms at GC-PC synapses, which are based on a small number of releasable SVs and a rapid Ca2+ driven recruitment of SVs.
evidence: Comparison of modeling predictions to experimental observations

claim: Several aspects of experimental findings, in particular high-frequency facilitation and LFD, can be reproduced by a simple sequential two-pool model with Ca2+-dependent recruitment.
source: Taken together, these findings show that several aspects of our experimental findings, in particular high-frequency facilitation and LFD, can be reproduced by a simple sequential two-pool model with Ca2+-dependent recruitment.
evidence: Summary of modeling results compared to experimental data

claim: Full recovery after LFD was described by a single exponential function (tau = 153.8 s, R2 = 0.93).
source: As shown in Figure 7A, full recovery after LFD was described by a single exponential function (tau = 153.8 s, R2 = 0.93), indicating a single-step process.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of recovery kinetics from experimental data

claim: Recovery following LFDtriplet followed a single exponential time course (tau = 212.8 s) but started with a long delay.
source: Recovery following LFDtriplet also followed a single exponential time course (tau = 212.8 s, Figure 7A) but started with a long delay.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of recovery kinetics after LFDtriplet

claim: A simple 90 s shift led to an identical monoexponential recovery in both LFD (mean tau = 156.3 s, R2 = 0.98, n = 8) and LFDtriplet (mean tau = 149.3 s, R2 = 0.96, n = 6).
source: Averaged time courses show that simple 90 s shift led to an identical monoexponential recovery in both LFD (mean tau = 156.3 s, R2 = 0.98, n = 8) and LFDtriplet (mean tau = 149.3 s, R2 = 0.96, n = 6) (Figure 7B,C).
evidence: Quantitative comparison of recovery kinetics with time shift

claim: The delay preceding the exponential recovery from depression after LFDtriplet (~90 s) may reflect the time required to reconstitute the reluctant pool.
source: The delay preceding the exponential recovery from depression after LFDtriplet (~90 s) may reflect the time required to reconstitute the reluctant pool.
evidence: Interpretation of experimental observation of delayed recovery

claim: After 1 min of rest following LFDtriplet, the first responses in the test train were still fully blocked whereas the amplitudes of the late responses were similar to the corresponding responses in the control train.
source: More interestingly, after 1 min of rest, the first responses in the test train were still fully blocked (Figure 7E) whereas the amplitudes of the late responses reflecting the recruitment of the releasable pool (after stimuli # 11–12 in the test train) were similar to the corresponding responses in the control train (Figure 7F).
evidence: Experimental observation from recovery protocols with variable rest periods

claim: After 1 min of rest following LFDtriplet, no SVs from the fully-releasable pool were ready to be released, despite partial reconstitution of the reluctant pool.
source: This demonstrates that even after 1 min of rest, no SVs from the fully-releasable pool were ready to be released, despite partial reconstitution of the reluctant pool.
evidence: Inference from experimental data showing differential recovery of pools

claim: An increase of [Ca2+]e from 2.5 mM to 4 mM can increase pr from 0.25 to 0.67 for SVs in the fully-releasable pool.
source: Based on our previous studies, we estimated that an increase of [Ca2+]e from 2.5 mM to 4 mM can increase pr from 0.25 to 0.67 for SVs in the fully-releasable pool (Valera et al., 2012).
evidence: Estimation based on previous experimental work

claim: In the presence of 4 mM [Ca2+]e, the number of quanta released during LFD almost doubled as compared to LFD elicited in 2.5 mM [Ca2+]e.
source: In the presence of 4 mM [Ca2+]e, the number of quanta released during LFD almost doubled as compared to LFD elicited in 2.5 mM [Ca2+]e (Figure 8A–C).
evidence: Experimental observation comparing quantal release at different Ca2+ concentrations

claim: The time course of normalized amplitudes of EPSCs during LFD was barely affected in high [Ca2+]e; neither the delay, nor the plateau of LFD or the decay time constant were statistically different in low and high Ca2+ conditions.
source: However, the time course of normalized amplitudes of EPSCs during LFD was barely affected in high [Ca2+]e; neither the delay, nor the plateau of LFD or the decay time constant were statistically different in low and high Ca2+ conditions (Figure 8D,E).
evidence: Statistical comparison of LFD parameters at different Ca2+ concentrations

claim: Similar mechanisms underlying LFD occur at low and high pr conditions.
source: This suggests that similar mechanisms underlying LFD occur at low and high pr conditions.
evidence: Inference from experimental data showing similar LFD kinetics at different Ca2+ levels

claim: The recovery from LFD was strongly reduced (maximal recovery 85.5%±11.6 n = 5) with high [Ca2+]e.
source: On the other hand, the recovery from LFD was strongly reduced (maximal recovery 85.5%±11.6 n = 5, Figure 8D) with high [Ca2+]e.
evidence: Experimental observation of reduced recovery at high Ca2+

claim: The reluctant pool was partially exhausted after LFD in high [Ca2+]e.
source: This indicates that the reluctant pool was partially exhausted after LFD in high [Ca2+]e.
evidence: Inference from reduced recovery at high Ca2+

claim: The increase in the number of quanta released during LFD in high [Ca2+]e probably arises from the recruitment of SVs in reluctant pool.
source: Hence, the increase in the number of quanta released during LFD in high [Ca2+]e probably arises from the recruitment of SVs in reluctant pool.
evidence: Inference from experimental observations of increased release and reduced recovery at high Ca2+

claim: Bath application of 10 µM EGTA-AM did not affect the basal release of glutamate.
source: Bath application of 10 µM EGTA-AM did not affect the basal release of glutamate (Figure 8F, Schmidt et al., 2013) and the time course of LFD (Figure 8F–H)
evidence: Experimental observation and citation of previous work

claim: Bath application of 10 µM EGTA-AM did not affect the time course of LFD.
source: Bath application of 10 µM EGTA-AM did not affect the basal release of glutamate (Figure 8F, Schmidt et al., 2013) and the time course of LFD (Figure 8F–H)
evidence: Experimental observation from EGTA-AM application experiments

claim: EGTA-AM application slowed-down and reduced the recovery from LFD during the first responses of the 100 Hz train.
source: whereas the recovery from LFD was slowed-down and reduced during the first responses of the 100 Hz train. Statistically significant differences were detected only at stimulus #4 and #5 of the train (p=0.031 for both stimuli, signed rank test, n = 6) (Figure 8G).
evidence: Statistical analysis of recovery with EGTA-AM application

claim: The reduction in the number of reluctant SVs recruited by a 100 Hz recovery train following an alteration of the spatiotemporal profile of Ca2+ confirms that one transition step from the reluctant state to the fully-releasable is Ca2+-dependent.
source: The reduction in the number of reluctant SVs recruited by a 100 Hz recovery train following an alteration of the spatiotemporal profile of Ca2+ confirms our simulation that suggests that one transition step from the reluctant state to the fully-releasable is Ca2+-dependent.
evidence: Experimental observation with EGTA-AM supporting modeling predictions

claim: The release of glutamate and the presynaptic short-term plasticity at GC-PC synapses are shaped by two pools of releasable SVs, namely fully-releasable SVs and reluctant SVs, which are differentially poised for exocytosis.
source: The present work demonstrates that the release of glutamate and the presynaptic short-term plasticity at GC-PC synapses are shaped by two pools of releasable SVs, namely fully-releasable SVs and reluctant SVs, which are differentially poised for exocytosis.
evidence: Summary statement of main finding from all experimental data

claim: The RRP is restricted to the fully-releasable pool, that is, to the only SVs that can be released by a single AP.
source: Here, we propose that the RRP is restricted to the fully-releasable pool, that is, to the only SVs that can be released by a single AP (see also Miki et al., 2016).
evidence: Proposed definition based on experimental findings and literature

claim: Stimulations of unitary GC-PC synapses and stimulations of beam of PFs gave similar values of the PPR.
source: Nevertheless, we previously showed that stimulations of unitary GC-PC synapses and stimulations of beam of PFs gave similar values of the PPR (Valera et al., 2012; Brachtendorf et al., 2015).
evidence: Reference to previous experimental work

claim: Most of GC terminals are equipped with both fully-releasable and reluctant pools.
source: Since the ultrafast recruitment of the reluctant pool underlies part of the strong paired-pulse facilitation observed at GC-PC synapses, we believe that most of GC terminals are equipped with both pools.
evidence: Inference from PPR data and previous findings

claim: The recruitment of reluctant SVs is achieved via both Ca2+-dependent and Ca2+-independent steps.
source: Our simulation and experimental findings show that the recruitment of reluctant SVs is achieved via both Ca2+-dependent and Ca2+-independent steps.
evidence: Conclusion from modeling and experimental data

claim: Synaptotagmin 7 is unlikely to play a role in the ultrafast recruitment of SVs from the reluctant pool because of the slow kinetics of its C2A domain.
source: Synaptotagmin 7 is unlikely to play a role in the ultrafast recruitment of SVs from the reluctant pool because of the slow kinetics of its C2A domain (Hui et al., 2005; Brandt et al., 2012 but see Jackman and Regehr, 2017).
evidence: Inference based on known kinetic properties from literature

claim: Munc13s are required in a superpriming step that may be analogous to the transition process described in this study.
source: Interestingly, Munc13s are required in a superpriming step that may be analogous to the transition process described in this study (Lee et al., 2013; Lipstein et al., 2013; Ishiyama et al., 2014).
evidence: Comparison to literature findings suggesting molecular mechanism

claim: At GC-PC synapses, filamentous proteins may serve as tracks or molecular motors driving reluctant SVs up to the fusion sites.
source: At GC-PC synapses, these filamentous proteins may serve as tracks or molecular motors driving reluctant SVs up to the fusion sites (Hallermann and Silver, 2013).
evidence: Speculative mechanism based on literature and current findings

claim: Both experimental data and simulations suggest that SVs can revert from the fully-releasable status back to the reluctant one.
source: Anyhow, both experimental data (Figure 7) and simulations (Figure 6) suggest that SVs can revert from the fully-releasable status back to the reluctant one, but it remains unclear why the equilibrium shifts toward the reluctant state at low frequencies.
evidence: Conclusion from experimental and modeling data

claim: The step back to the reluctant state may correspond to an 'a posteriori' mechanism impeding the functioning of active release sites in the low-frequency range.
source: The step back to the reluctant state may correspond to an 'a posteriori' mechanism impeding the functioning of active release sites in the low-frequency range (Wölfel et al., 2007; Schneggenburger et al., 2012).
evidence: Speculative mechanism based on literature models

claim: LFD may arise from an imbalance in the activation of presynaptic kinases and phosphatases and as such the kinase/phosphatase balance would act as a frequency sensor regulating the equilibrium between the two pools.
source: On the other hand, as proposed for invertebrate synapses (Silverman-Gavrila et al., 2005; Doussau et al., 2010), LFD may arise from an imbalance in the activation of presynaptic kinases and phosphatases and as such the kinase/phosphatase balance would act as a frequency sensor regulating the equilibrium between the two pools.
evidence: Speculative mechanism based on literature from other synapses

claim: The number of SVs that can be released during high-frequency trains after a full depletion of fully-releasable SVs corresponds to the size of the reluctant pool.
source: Our calculations indicate that the number of SVs that can be released during high-frequency trains after a full depletion of fully-releasable SVs corresponds to the size of the reluctant pool (Figure 4).
evidence: Calculation based on experimental data

claim: The two releasable pools are refilled by other pools (recycling pool, reserve pool) during LFD, LFDtriplet and during the late phase of high-frequency trains.
source: Since the number of SVs released per bouton (30–40 SVs, Figures 1 and 4) during 50/100 Hz trains, LFD, LFDtriplet or during recovery trains far exceeds the number of docked SVs counted in one varicosity at GC-PC synapses (4–8 SVs, Xu-Friedman et al., 2001), we postulate that the two releasable pools are refilled by other pools (recycling pool, reserve pool) during LFD, LFDtriplet and during the late phase of high-frequency trains.
evidence: Inference from comparison of released SVs to anatomical counts

claim: MF-GC synapses can sustain high frequency trains of input by using a specific arrangement of the presynaptic machinery to achieve ultra-fast reloading of SVs.
source: Strikingly, MF-GC synapses can sustain high frequency trains of input by using a specific arrangement of the presynaptic machinery to achieve ultra-fast reloading of SVs (Saviane and Silver, 2006; Rancz et al., 2007; Hallermann et al., 2010; Ritzau-Jost et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple literature citations

claim: During a train of APs at high frequency, the local [Ca2+] at release sites increases leading to an immediate increase in the number of release sites N.
source: During a train of APs at high frequency, the local [Ca2+] at release sites increases (Schmidt et al., 2013) leading to an immediate increase in the number of release sites N that underlies high values of paired-pulse facilitation (Valera et al., 2012; Brachtendorf et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement based on previous experimental work

claim: The increase in N during high-frequency trains arises from the fast recruitment of reluctant SVs into a fully-releasable pool.
source: Here, we show that this increase in N arises from the fast recruitment of reluctant SVs into a fully-releasable pool.
evidence: Conclusion from current experimental findings

claim: A fast and sequential recruitment of a 'replacement pool' in 'a docked pool' accounting for paired-pulse facilitation has been recently described at GC-MLI synapses.
source: A fast and sequential recruitment of a 'replacement pool' in 'a docked pool' accounting for paired-pulse facilitation has been recently described at GC-MLI synapses (Miki et al., 2016).
evidence: Statement from literature describing similar mechanism at different synapse

claim: The GC-PC synapse is unique because it allows for inactivation of the fully-releasable pool by low-frequency stimulation.
source: The GC-PC synapse is unique, because it allows for inactivation of the fully-releasable pool by low-frequency stimulation.
evidence: Conclusion from experimental findings showing LFD

claim: The combination of LFD and reluctant pool recruitment endows GC-PC synapses with the striking ability to filter repetitive activities around 2 Hz and to invert the orientation of presynaptic plasticity depending on the stimulation frequency.
source: The combination of both mechanisms endows these synapses with the striking ability to filter repetitive activities around 2 Hz and to invert the orientation of presynaptic plasticity (full depression versus strong facilitation) depending on the stimulation frequency (Figure 2).
evidence: Conclusion from experimental observations of frequency-dependent plasticity

claim: During high-frequency inputs, GC-PC synapses are able to set the release glutamate independently of the state of the synapse (synapse at rest or depressed synapse).
source: Finally, during high-frequency inputs, GC-PC synapses are able to set the release glutamate independently of the state of the synapse (synapse at rest or depressed synapse) (Figure 2).
evidence: Conclusion from experimental data showing similar recovery regardless of initial state

claim: In lobules IV and V, GCs responding to joint rotation fire spontaneously at 2–10 Hz due to sustained synaptic inputs from MFs.
source: In vivo experiments have shown that in lobules IV and V, GCs responding to joint rotation fire spontaneously at 2–10 Hz due to sustained synaptic inputs from MFs.
evidence: Statement based on in vivo experimental literature

claim: Upon joint movement, GC firing rate shifts instantaneously into burst mode with frequencies ranging from approximately 50 Hz to 300 Hz.
source: Upon joint movement, their firing rate shifts instantaneously into burst mode with frequencies ranging from ~50 Hz to 300 Hz (Jörntell and Ekerot, 2006).
evidence: Statement from in vivo recording literature

claim: In the absence of sensory activity, GC inputs to PCs are silenced as most SVs are in the reluctant state.
source: Based on our work, we propose that GC-PC synapses filter GC activity. In the absence of sensory activity, GC inputs to PCs are silenced as most SVs are in the reluctant state.
evidence: Proposed physiological model based on experimental findings

claim: During joint movement, the efficient transmission of high-frequency activity from MF to GC and from GC to PC is enabled by the recruitment of the reluctant pool at GC-PC terminals.
source: During joint movement, the efficient transmission of high-frequency activity from MF to GC (Saviane and Silver, 2006; Rancz et al., 2007; Hallermann et al., 2010) and from GC to PC (Valera et al., 2012) is enabled by the recruitment of the reluctant pool at GC-PC terminals.
evidence: Proposed physiological model integrating current findings with literature

claim: The efficient filtering of low-frequency activity would enhance the signal to noise ratio and enable PCs to discern sensory signals from spontaneous activity in GCs.
source: The efficient filtering of low-frequency activity would enhance the signal to noise ratio and enable PCs to discern sensory signals from spontaneous activity in GCs.
evidence: Proposed functional consequence of experimental findings

claim: At the calyx of Held, the RRP can be separated into a fast-releasing pool (FRP) and a slowly releasing one (SRP).
source: In the calyx of Held, for example, the RRP can be separated into a fast-releasing pool (FRP) and a slowly releasing one (SRP) (Sakaba and Neher, 2001; Sakaba, 2006; Schneggenburger et al., 2012).
evidence: Statement from literature about other synapses

claim: At the calyx of Held, during a train of APs, SRP vesicles are first converted into FRP vesicles and then mature to a fully-releasable state.
source: During a train of APs, SRP vesicles are first converted into FRP vesicles and then mature to a fully-releasable state (Lee et al., 2012, 2013).
evidence: Statement from literature describing mechanism at calyx of Held

claim: At synapses between granule cells (GCs) and molecular layer interneurons (MLIs), two subsets of the RRP have been described that are mobilized by a two-step process.
source: In the cerebellar cortex, at synapses between granule cells (GCs) and molecular layer interneurons (MLIs), two subsets of the RRP have been described that are also mobilized by a two-step process, although the transition is faster than at the Calyx of Held (Ishiyama et al., 2014; Miki et al., 2016).
evidence: Statement from literature about cerebellar synapses

claim: At the calyx of Held with a very large RRP (700 to 5000 SVs) synaptic transmission quickly depresses.
source: Counter-intuitively, the size of the RRP does not determine the direction of presynaptic plasticity during high-frequency stimulation; at the calyx of Held with a very large RRP (700 to 5000 SVs; Borst and Soria van Hoeve, 2012) synaptic transmission quickly depresses
evidence: Statement from literature about calyx of Held properties

claim: At the GC to PC synapse, synaptic transmission facilitates during tens of APs despite a small RRP (4–8 SVs) and a relatively high pr.
source: whereas at the GC to Purkinje cell (PC) synapse, synaptic transmission facilitates during tens of APs (Kreitzer and Regehr, 2000; Valera et al., 2012; Schmidt et al., 2013) despite a small RRP (4–8 SVs, Xu-Friedman et al., 2001) and a relatively high pr (Schmidt et al., 2013; Sims and Hartell, 2005; Valera et al., 2012 - but see Atluri and Regehr, 1996).
evidence: Statement integrating multiple literature sources about GC-PC synapse properties

claim: The striking facilitation at GC-PC synapses is mediated by an increase in the number of release sites within milliseconds upon a Ca2+-dependent process.
source: Using computer simulations combined with variance-mean analysis of postsynaptic responses, we previously showed that this striking facilitation is mediated by an increase in the number of release sites within milliseconds upon a Ca2+-dependent process (Valera et al., 2012; Brachtendorf et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement from previous work by the authors

claim: The RRP comprises heterogeneous populations of SVs that are differently poised for exocytosis and sequentially recruited for exocytosis.
source: Besides, there is increasing evidence that the RRP comprises heterogeneous populations of SVs that are differently poised for exocytosis and sequentially recruited for exocytosis.
evidence: Statement summarizing literature evidence

claim: Short-term plasticity during high-frequency trains is shaped by the differential mobilization of sub-pools of SVs in the RRP.
source: Together, these studies suggest that short-term plasticity during high-frequency trains is shaped by the differential mobilization of sub-pools of SVs in the RRP (Pan and Zucker, 2009; Miki et al., 2016).
evidence: Conclusion from literature review
